# Hardware Collision Kill Switch for Strain Wave Mounts

The proposal: a normally-closed switch on the camera or OTA. Pressing it
cuts DC power to the mount, and power stays off until someone intervenes
by hand. It is independent of software and meant to protect against
collisions with a tripod or pier, which strain wave torque makes costly.
This topic looks for prior art, tests whether the design's premise holds,
and collects requirements.

**Bottom line:**

1. **Not found as specified.** No product or reported build matches the
   exact design. The principle (hardware sensors cutting mount power
   independently of software) has been discussed since at least 2016 [86]
   and endorsed on Cloudy Nights [1], [2].
   - Position-triggered and communication-loss power cutters exist [3], [4],
     [85]; after a crash [6], one Wave 150i owner built and tested a
     reed-switch cutoff [85].
   - The closest suggestion is a pier-mounted micro switch the scope touches,
     wired in the mount's 12V line; it was not reported as built [85].
   - Professional radio telescopes reportedly used struck micro-switches
     with manual recovery [2].
   - The one posted amateur schematic appears to be neither fail-safe nor
     latching as drawn. This is our reading of the drawing [93].
2. **The premise needs care.** Most documented strain wave brakes cover
   **RA only**: ZWO AM5/AM3 [21], [29], [31], Pegasus NYX-101 [36],
   SAL-33 [39]. An unbraked DEC can move when unpowered [21], [36].
   Back-drivability sources conflict [54], [55], [56]. A single-user AM5
   teardown puts the brake on the stepper; by inference, a belt failure
   would defeat it. With the brake
   removed, a 14 lb load did not fall by itself but kept going once pushed
   [88].

## Key table

| Question | Answer | Key sources |
|---|---|---|
| Does the exact device exist? | Not found in this source pool | [prior art](references/prior-art.md) |
| Closest relatives | Radio-telescope push-to-break limit switches (recalled); pier micro switch in the 12V line (suggested); AP1200 accelerometer relay; MountWatcher comms-loss relay; Wave 150i reed-switch cutoff (built); 2016 relay limit-switch recommendation | [1]–[5], [85], [86] |
| Do strain wave mounts hold position unpowered? | RA usually (brake); DEC often unbraked. iOptron HAE brakes both axes. | [21], [29], [34], [36] |
| Is a hard cut mid-slew safe? | Disputed: iOptron ("safely stop") and Pegasus ("instant safe stop") describe brake stops as safe; Rainbow says don't; industry says holding brakes are not stopping brakes | [34], [36], [37], [58] |
| Does the mount detect collisions itself? | AM5: stall detection only at 1440x, not while tracking (ZWO staff). RST-135: load monitoring cuts power. | [22], [37] |
| Position after the cut | AM5: no absolute encoders, re-home (forum report). iOptron HAE and NYX-101 store position. | [34], [36], [40] |

## Decision framework

1. **Check your mount's brake axes.** If DEC is unbraked (AM5, AM3,
   NYX-101, SAL-33), balance DEC and test a power cut indoors before relying
   on the switch [21], [36], [40].
2. **Keep limits.** The switch complements firmware and software limits;
   it does not replace them (ISO 13850 §4.1.1.3) [68]. ISO 13850 covers
   E-stops started by "a single human action" [68], so its clauses apply
   here by analogy only.
3. **Design the switch as a latching NC trip.** Use NC, positive-opening
   contacts, placed downstream of every controller in the power path, with
   no command able to override it [8], [68], [76], [77], [80]. The one posted
   amateur schematic, as we read it, trips by energizing a relay and resets
   by itself. Avoid that pattern [93].
4. **Make re-enable a separate, deliberate step.** Clear the obstacle,
   reset at the device, confirm the mount does not auto-resume tracking,
   then re-home or resync [44], [68], [70], [73].
5. **Accept the residual risk.** A contact trip fires after contact.
   Ratcheting can happen in milliseconds [63]. The switch bounds how long
   the force lasts, not the first impact.
